examples.question_text:
Use the dot product to determine whether each pair of vectors is perpendicular.

(a) $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}15\\-6\end{pmatrix}$.

(b) $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
examples.solution_text:
(a)

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{u}\cdot\underset{\sim}{v}&=(2)(15)+(5)(-6)\\&=30-30\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both vectors are non-zero and their dot product is zero, so they are perpendicular.

(b)

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}&=(4)(2)+(-3)(5)\\&=8-15\\&=-7\end{aligned}$

The dot product is not zero, so these vectors are not perpendicular.

Perpendicular non-zero vectors have dot product zero.

$\begin{aligned}(3)(m)+(7)(-6)&=0\\3m-42&=0\\3m&=42\\m&=14\end{aligned}$

Neither vector is zero when $m=14$, so this value is valid.

Use vectors starting at the angle's vertex, $B$.

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{BA}&=\begin{pmatrix}1-5\\2-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\\\overrightarrow{BC}&=\begin{pmatrix}3-5\\8-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}&=(-4)(-2)+(-2)(4)\\&=8-8\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both vectors are non-zero, so $\overrightarrow{BA}\perp\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$.

examples.question_text: Find all values of $t$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}t\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}t+3\\-7\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
examples.solution_text:
Set the dot product equal to zero.

$\begin{aligned}(t)(t+3)+(4)(-7)&=0\\t^{2}+3t-28&=0\\(t+7)(t-4)&=0\end{aligned}$

$t=-7$ or $t=4$.

The fixed components $4$ and $-7$ ensure both vectors are non-zero, so both values are valid.

examples.question_text: Find all values of $k$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}k-4\\k-4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\2\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
examples.solution_text:
First solve the zero-dot-product equation.

$\begin{aligned}(k-4)k+(k-4)(2)&=0\\(k-4)(k+2)&=0\end{aligned}$

$k=4$ or $k=-2$.

When $k=4$, $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The zero vector has no direction, so reject this value.

When $k=-2$, $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Both are non-zero and their dot product is zero.

Therefore, $k=-2$ only.

examples.derivation: Independently calculated (a) 2×15+5×(−6)=30−30=0 and (b) 4×2+(−3)×5=8−15=−7. All vectors are non-zero; only pair (a) is perpendicular. This follows the component test in source lines 619–637.

The perpendicularity equation is 3m+7×(−6)=0, giving 3m=42 and m=14. Both vectors remain non-zero. The algebraic substitution and equation-solving method is supported by source lines 210–227 and 718–728.

Subtracting coordinates gives BA=(−4,−2) and BC=(−2,4). Their dot product is 8−8=0. Both are non-zero and start at B, proving angle ABC=90°. The TikZ vertices match the stated coordinates, with black outlines and labels and no derived answer annotation. Coordinate subtraction followed by a perpendicularity test is supported by source lines 794–815.

The dot product equation is t(t+3)−28=0. Factoring t²+3t−28 gives (t+7)(t−4)=0, so t=−7 or 4. The fixed second components prevent either vector from being zero. This matches the quadratic perpendicularity method in source lines 718–728.

The dot product factors as (k−4)k+2(k−4)=(k−4)(k+2), producing k=4 or −2. At k=4 the first vector is zero, so that root is rejected. At k=−2 the vectors are (−6,−6) and (−2,2), with dot product 12−12=0. Thus k=−2 only. Factoring follows source lines 718–728; exclusion follows the non-zero condition in lines 85–87.
